subject: physics_2

verification.note: The 1+1+1+1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. For this paper the two-book union check and the past-paper back-test are both STRUCTURALLY IMPOSSIBLE: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is first-year physics only, and the paper corpus holds only Paper-I papers. Physics hand-checked: dB ∝ i, dB ∝ dl, dB ∝ sin θ, dB ∝ 1/r², so dB = (μ₀/4π)(i dl sin θ)/r², with μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ — matches the book. The book's printed question reads 'Biot savart law'; the proper name is corrected here to 'Biot-Savart'. In the figure dB at P is into the page, which follows from dl × r with the current upward and P to the right and below.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.
insider_note: Write the four proportionalities as four numbered lines before you combine them. Examiners mark them one by one, and a student who jumps straight to the final formula loses the middle marks.

steps.label: The current element and the point P
steps.margin_note: A wire carrying current i, one small element dl on it, the point P at distance r, and the angle θ between the element and the line to P.
steps.why: Every symbol in the formula is a marked part of this one picture, so drawing it first makes the four proportionalities read straight off the figure.
common_mistakes: Marking θ at P instead of at the element. The angle sits between the element and the line joining the element to P.
Drawing r from the bottom of the wire. It runs from the mid-point of the element to P.

recall.must_convey: That a wire with a small element dl is drawn, with r to the point P and the angle θ between them marked.
accept: draw the wire and a small element dl
mark r from the element to P
reject: dB is mu nought by four pi

steps.memory_tip: One wire, one short element, one line out to P: dl, r and θ are all on that line.

steps.label: The set-up and the statement
lines: Take a small element of length dl of a wire
carrying a current i. Let P be a point at a
distance r from the element, and let θ be the
angle between the element and the line
joining the element to P.
Biot-Savart law: the magnetic induction dB at
P due to this element is directly
proportional to the current, to the length of
the element and to sin θ, and is inversely
proportional to the square of r.
steps.margin_note: First mark. Name dl, r and θ, then say the four dependences in words before writing any symbol.
steps.why: The law is about ONE small piece of the wire, not the whole wire: the field of a full circuit is found by adding the dB of every element.
common_mistakes: Applying the law to the whole wire at once. It gives dB for one element only.
Measuring r from the point P to the wire's end instead of to the element.

recall.must_convey: That dB at P from a current element depends on i, dl, sin θ and 1/r².
accept: field due to a small current element
depends on current length and sine theta
inversely as the square of the distance

steps.memory_tip: Three things on top (i, dl, sin θ) and one thing below (r²).

steps.label: The four proportionalities
lines: 1) directly proportional to the current i:
2) directly proportional to the length dl:
3) directly proportional to sin θ:
4) inversely proportional to r²:
steps.margin_note: Second mark. Four numbered lines, one for each dependence — this is the part examiners tick one by one.
steps.why: Each line is a separate experimental fact, so writing them apart shows where every factor in the final formula comes from.
common_mistakes: Writing cos θ in place of sin θ. The element and the line to P give sin θ.
Writing 1/r instead of 1/r². It is an inverse square law.

recall.must_convey: The four separate proportionalities: to i, to dl, to sin θ and to 1/r².
accept: dB proportional to one by r squared
reject: the angle is between the element and the line to P

steps.memory_tip: Count them off on four fingers: i, dl, sin θ, then r² underneath.

steps.label: Combining them
lines: Putting the four results together,

lines.text: dB ∝ i dl sin θ / r²

lines: Writing the constant of proportionality as
μ₀/4π for a wire in vacuum,

lines.text: dB = (μ₀/4π) · i dl sin θ / r²

steps.margin_note: Third mark. Multiply the three top factors, divide by r², then put in the constant μ₀/4π.
steps.why: A proportionality becomes an equation only when a constant is fixed; μ₀/4π is the constant that makes the SI units come out in tesla.
common_mistakes: Writing the constant as μ₀ alone. It is μ₀/4π.
Dropping sin θ once the constant is put in.

recall.must_convey: That the four results combine to dB ∝ i dl sin θ / r², and the constant is μ₀/4π.
accept: dB proportional to i dl sine theta by r squared
constant is mu nought by four pi
reject: mu nought is four pi into ten power minus seven

steps.memory_tip: Multiply the three that raise dB, divide by the one that lowers it.

steps.label: The final formula
steps.mark_note: dB = (μ₀/4π) i dl sin θ / r²

lines.text: dB = (μ₀/4π) · i dl sin θ / r²

lines: Here μ₀ = 4π × 10⁻⁷ T m A⁻¹ is the
permeability of free space.
dB is perpendicular to the plane containing
the element and the line to P. In vector form
In the figure dB at P is into the page (⊗).
steps.margin_note: Last mark. The boxed formula, the value of μ₀ and one line on the direction of dB.
steps.why: The cross product is what fixes the direction: dB is perpendicular to both the element and the line to P, which is why the field of a straight wire circles the wire.
common_mistakes: Leaving out the units of μ₀ when its value is asked for.
Saying dB points from the element towards P. It is perpendicular to that line.

recall.must_convey: The final formula dB = (μ₀/4π) i dl sin θ / r², and that dB is perpendicular to the plane of dl and r.
accept: dB equals mu nought by four pi i dl sine theta by r squared
dB is perpendicular to the plane

steps.memory_tip: Same shape as Coulomb's law: a constant, the source on top, r² below.
